What do you need the tool to do first?

See stepsSee stepsSee steps

Get suggestions in your editor or try an agent-first editor

Start with GitHub Copilot if your first task is accepting and editing suggestions in a supported editor you already use. Try Cursor if you also want to hand off edits and review proposed changes inside its editor. Both products offer more than one mode, so verify the exact mode you intend to use.

Try the same short function and two call sites in each editor. Check how quickly you can see, edit and undo the proposed changes. If you are evaluating inline completion alone, use that same mode for both tools.

Delegate a repository fix from the terminal

Try Codex CLI or Claude Code if your first task is reading a codebase and preparing a patch. Start in a separate checkout with a single scoped task. Check which files it proposes to change and what permission is needed to run tests.

Use the same starting code and prompt per attempt. Record the client, model or provider shown, any extra instructions and the time spent reviewing. The Claude Code and Cursor trial kit also records the execution and sign-in limits of the retained experiment.

Choose a model provider, or start from one concrete task

OpenCode is a starting point if you need to select a supported model provider. Verify the active model and provider before pasting any repository content. The OpenCode project guide covers permissions and practical checks.

If your workflow is still unclear, pick the smallest task you repeat. Try an inline completion for frequent small edits, or the bounded repair exercise below for delegated changes. Review what information each tool sends to its provider before using it on private code.

Run the same repair trial and score the patch yourself

  1. Download the starter repository and prompt. Extract it separately for each tool and use Node.js 22 or newer.
  2. From the fixture directory, run node --test test/orders.test.mjs before changing anything. The retained starter run passed 2 of 12 checks.
  3. Give each tool the prompt. Read its patch before executing it, and verify the supplied tests and README are unchanged. Run the original checks yourself.
  4. Download the supplementary checks and save them in the fixture directory. Run the command below after reviewing the implementation. It imports and executes the file you name, so use a reviewed copy in an isolated directory.
node check-orders.mjs src/orders.mjs

The output lists pass or fail for each contract check and returns a failure code if any check fails. Keep this result beside the original test report and note what needed manual correction. Save a side-by-side record with the trial log.

What the eight extra checks caught

On November 28, we ran eight contract checks against the retained first patch from the November 27 trial and the author’s reference. The first patch had passed 12 of 12 original tests. It passed 4 of 8 additional checks, accepting a numeric ID, numeric amount, array amount and null refund. The reference passed all eight.

First patch results · Reference results

The November 27 patch came from a configured Claude Code CLI with a reported third-party model label. Cursor generation was untested. This exercise shows where the original tests left gaps in one patch. The shortlist above uses documented workflows, and the checks help you test the tools with your own settings.
